conceptTag: Is the effect big enough to matter?
readerTitle: The test worked. The rollout would have lost money.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (상업용 청소 회사, 레스토랑) + 실제 연구 (미국통계학회 2016년 p값 성명)
insight: 효과가 '진짜인가'와 '할 가치가 있는가'는 다른 질문이다. 효과의 크기를 규모와 비용 옆에 놓고 돈으로 환산해야 결정할 수 있다.
misconception: 테스트에서 효과가 우연이 아니라고 확인되면 도입하면 된다. 반대로 작은 효과는 무시해도 된다.

sources.text: Wasserstein, R. L. & Lazar, N. A. (2016). The ASA Statement on p-Values: Context, Process, and Purpose. The American Statistician, 70(2).
청소 회사와 레스토랑의 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 레스토랑 계산: 월 6,000테이블 × 2%p = 디저트 120개 추가 × 공헌이익 $4 = 월 $480, 연 약 $5,760.
ASA 성명의 원칙 5 문구('A p-value, or statistical significance, does not measure the size of an effect or the importance of a result')를 게시 전 원문과 대조하세요. 카드에는 의역으로 적었습니다.

cards.title: The test worked. The rollout would have lost money.
body: A cleaning company ran a careful year-long test. Check-in calls really did keep more clients from leaving. The result was not luck.
Rolling the calls out to every client would still have cost about $48,000 a year.
Being sure an effect exists is one question. Knowing it's worth having is another.

image.label: A trophy labeled 'Proven' sitting on a shrinking pile of coins
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 'Proven'이라고 적힌 작은 트로피가 동전 더미 위에 놓여 있고, 동전 더미 아래쪽이 조금씩 새어 나가는 모습. 실제 기업 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: The check-in calls are a proven winner.
body: You run a commercial cleaning company with 4,000 office clients. For a year, half got a check-in call every quarter. The other half didn't.
Cancellations: 10% without calls, 8% with calls. Your analyst confirms the gap is real, not chance. What do you do next?

options.text: Roll the calls out to every client. The test proved they work
options.feedback: You act on a real effect, but you skip the question of what it's worth. Proven and profitable are not the same thing.

options.text: Put a dollar value on the 2-point drop and compare it with the cost of the calls
options.feedback: This turns 'it works' into 'it pays' or 'it doesn't'. It takes an hour of math and can save a costly rollout.

options.text: Run the test another year to be even more certain
options.feedback: More data shrinks your doubt about whether the effect is real. But that doubt is already small. The open question is size versus cost.

cards.title: Price the effect.
body: Each kept client earns about $2,400 a year in profit. Each call costs about $15 in staff time. The effect is real, and it is **smaller than its cost**.

breakdown.label: Net per year
breakdown.detail: A real effect that loses money

cards.title: Real is not the same as big enough
body: A test answers two different questions. *Is the effect real?* That's what "statistically significant" means: the result is unlikely to be pure chance.
*Is it big enough to matter?* That's **practical significance**. You find it by turning the effect into money, time or customers, then setting it against the cost of getting it.
The cleaning test passed the first question and failed the second.

image.label: Two gates: 'Is it real?' and 'Is it worth it?'
image.brief: 길 위에 문 두 개가 차례로 서 있는 인포그래픽. 첫 번째 문 'Is it real?'은 열려 있고, 두 번째 문 'Is it worth it?' 앞에 저울(왼쪽 'Effect × scale', 오른쪽 'Cost')이 놓여 있음.

cards.softwareNote: With thousands of users, a tiny lift, like 0.1% more sign-ups, can pass as "significant". Ask what that lift earns per year, then compare it with the engineering and upkeep the change needs.

cards.title: Statisticians made this point officially.
body: In 2016, the American Statistical Association issued a formal statement on how test results get misread. One of its six principles: a p-value, the usual measure of "significance", does not tell you how large an effect is or how important it is.
The reason is simple. With enough data, even a trivial difference becomes measurable. Significance tells you how sure you can be. Only the size, in real units, tells you whether to care.

cards.title: Small isn't bad. Big isn't good.
body: Size only means something next to scale and cost:
list: **Small effect, almost free:** often worth doing
**Big effect, very expensive:** may still lose money
**Small effect, huge volume:** can add up to a lot
cards.callout: The real test: effect × how often it happens − what it costs.
cards.softwareNote: In software, the cost side is easy to forget. A change that adds code also adds testing, support and future maintenance for years.

cards.title: Your math can be too harsh.
body: Count the full value. A kept cleaning client may stay for years, not one. At three years of profit, the calls might pay off.
Look for a cheaper version. A check-in email at $1 might keep most of the effect for a fraction of the cost.
And remember that measured effects are estimates. Work out the result at the low and high end of the likely range before you decide.

cards.title: Now it's three restaurants.
body: Your servers tested one extra line at the end of the meal: "Our pastry chef made a lemon tart today." Dessert orders rose from 20% of tables to 22%.
You serve about 6,000 tables a month. Each dessert leaves about $4 after its costs. What do you do?

options.text: Drop it. Two points is too small to bother with
options.feedback: Small, yes. But 120 extra desserts a month is about $480 for a sentence that costs nothing. You'd give up free money.

options.text: Make the line standard. It costs almost nothing
options.feedback: A small effect against a near-zero cost is a clear win, about $5,700 a year. Keep an eye on whether guests start to find it pushy.

options.text: Hire a dessert server for $2,500 a month to push harder
options.feedback: You'd need the effect to grow more than fivefold just to break even. Scaling the cost doesn't scale the effect.

cards.title: Ask "how much is it worth?" not just "does it work?"
body: A real effect can lose money, and a tiny one can be a bargain. The decision comes from putting the size in dollars next to the cost.
**Try it today:** pick one change you made because "it worked". Write down the effect in dollars per year and what it costs to keep doing.
